old_title: Banton's ascent to England leadership role vindicates all-in approach to white-ball game
new_title: Banton's ascent to England leadership role vindicates all-in approach to white-ball game
old_text:
When Will Jacks broke his hand at the MCG last Saturday night - his birthday ruined and his tour of Australia over - there were a few directions England could have turned as regards the vice-captaincy.
Plenty of teams happily do without an official deputy, of course. But with Harry Brook jetting off to join the Test tour of South Africa after the fourth of these five T20 internationals, a replacement will be required when the series wraps up in Canberra.
Phil Salt was one option. For all of his unfettered aggression, powered by those tattooed, Popeye-like forearms, the opener is an intelligent, thoughtful cricketer very much in tune with the rhythms of T20. As well as two seasons captaining in the Hundred, most recently with Welsh Fire, Salt previously deputised for Jos Buttler against Australia at home two years ago.
And then there was Sam Curran, who has captained in the T20 Blast, the ILT20, the Hundred and, given its intensity and profile, most notably the Indian Premier League. Player of the tournament during England's T20 World Cup win here back in 2024 - Sam Curran MBE, no less - the all-rounder could easily have been asked.
England have instead turned to Tom Banton, eight years since he led the England Under-19s during a home summer series against South Africa and with just a handful of matches in charge of Taunton in the West of England Premier League in between. It says something about a cricketer whose stock is currently on the rise in the eyes of Brook and head coach Brendon McCullum.
"I was pretty emotional when I got told a few days ago in the airport," said Banton, ahead of Friday's third T20 at the Gabba. "To captain your country is a great honour and something I'm looking forward to. Baz [McCullum] told me in the airport, he just pulled me aside and told me. I didn't know how to react if I'm honest."
While it was McCullum who broke the news, this initial promotion to vice-captain is as much about Banton's tight relationship with Brook and Jacks. Former teammates during the 2018 Under-19s World Cup, they are clearly the new core of this white-ball set-up. Banton made his senior debut first, seven years ago, but it is only over the past 18 months that he has become as central as the other two.
Test ambitions also flickered at the start of 2025 when Banton's epic 371 against Worcestershire broke Somerset's record first-class score, previously held by Justin Langer (342). Key to that innings was his decision to dispense with dog-stick throwdowns in the nets, which he personally felt had led to bad habits.
However, last summer Banton put red-ball cricket on hold to go all-in on white-ball cricket. Whether causation or correlation, he has struck a rich run of form since, averaging 53 across 20 limited overs internationals and finishing player of the series during England's recent 2-1 win in the one-dayers. In this T20 series, a strike-rate of 216 again underlines how big he is seeing the white Kookaburra.
It is a sabbatical of sorts, with Banton honest about his desire to seek overseas franchise cricket outside of England commitments but keen to return to four-day cricket in time. Equally, if approached by a younger teammate considering the same move, the 28-year-old said he would "definitely advise pursuing it".
Banton's own mentor is the currently sidelined Buttler - "To have him at the other end of the phone is something I don't take for granted," he said - while Kevin Pietersen's recent presence in the England set-up as a "special mentor" during the first fortnight on tour was another welcome source of input.
"To have an idol of mine - and I'm sure many of the others - has been pretty awesome," Banton said. "He put a real emphasis on not just turning up to training for the sake of it. It has been really testing the nets.
"It is challenging and it can be quite scary at times. But as a group we're definitely seeing the rewards. The 10-day training block we had [in Perth] before the 50-over series ... I've never seen an England team train as hard as that."
That final observation is an interesting one, coming in Brisbane and exactly a year since Ben Stokes drove a push for England's players to undergo extra training in response to going 1-0 down in the Ashes. McCullum then famously argued they were in fact "over-prepared" after this became a ruinous 2-0 at the Gabba.
It was the first clear sign of a captain and coach going their separate ways by way of outlook and the rest, as they say, is history. For now though, albeit on a much lower-profile white-ball tour, England's leadership appears on the same page.
